questions.stem: Meera of Surat Saree House wants her shop's events converted into accounting information. The FIRST step of the accounting process is:

options.text: Recording the transactions in the journal
options.explanation: Recording is the third step — before anything reaches the journal, the events must first be picked out and expressed in money.

options.text: Identifying transactions and events of a financial character
options.explanation: Correct. The process begins by identifying which happenings are money-measurable transactions or events; only those enter the system at all.
Classifying comes after recording — entries must exist in the journal before they can be grouped in the ledger.
The trial balance belongs to the summarising stage, well after identifying, measuring, recording and classifying.

questions.sourceRef: Accounting process order: identify → measure → record → classify → summarise → analyse → interpret → communicate

questions.stem: All of Ram's dealings with the business are brought together in one place — Ram's account. This CLASSIFYING work happens in the:

options.explanation: The journal records chronologically, mixing all parties date-wise — it does not group one person's dealings together.
Correct. Classification means grouping entries of one kind in one account — and the book of accounts is the ledger.
The trial balance is a summarising device — it lists the ledger balances but does not do the grouping itself.
The Balance Sheet is a final summarised statement, two stages after classification.

questions.sourceRef: Classifying happens in the ledger; recording in journal; summarising in trial balance and final accounts

questions.stem: An accountant at Nair Spices first works out the ratio of profit to sales, and then explains to the owner what that ratio says about the firm's earning strength. The two steps performed, in order, are:

options.explanation: Correct. Analysing establishes relationships between figures (profit to sales); interpreting explains what those relationships mean — two distinct steps in that order.
Reversed — a relationship must be established (analysis) before its significance can be explained (interpretation).
Summarising condenses the ledger into statements; ratio work on those statements is a later, different step.
Those steps organise raw entries — they involve no ratios and no explanation of meaning.

questions.sourceRef: Analysing establishes relationships; interpreting explains their significance

questions.stem: Writing transactions chronologically in the journal and its subsidiary books belongs to which stage of the accounting process?

options.explanation: Classifying is the ledger's job — grouping like entries in one account, after they are recorded.
Summarising condenses ledger balances into the trial balance and final accounts — the journal is far upstream of that.
Correct. The journal and subsidiary books are the books of original entry — the chronological write-up is the recording stage.
Identifying merely picks out which events are financial in character — nothing is written in any book yet.

questions.sourceRef: Recording = journal and subsidiary books (books of original entry)

questions.stem: The classic definition of accounting as 'the art of recording, classifying and summarising … and interpreting the results thereof' was given by:

options.text: The AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants)
options.explanation: Correct. The classic definition comes from the American institute, and the ICAI Study Material opens with the same idea.
The ICAI's SM quotes and builds on the definition, but the definition itself originated with the American institute.
The Companies Act regulates companies; it does not supply the textbook definition of accounting.
The RBI is the banking regulator — it has nothing to do with defining accounting.

questions.sourceRef: AICPA classic definition of accounting

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Book-keeping vs accounting
questions.stem: Which statement about book-keeping and accounting is CORRECT?

options.explanation: Reversed — book-keeping is the primary (base) stage and accounting is the secondary stage built on it.

options.text: Book-keeping and accounting are two names for the same work
options.explanation: They differ in scope, stage, objective and nature of work — book-keeping is routine and clerical, accounting is analytical.

options.text: Book-keeping includes analysing and interpreting the results
options.explanation: Analysis and interpretation are exactly the parts that belong to accounting, not book-keeping.
Correct. Book-keeping covers the routine base work (identifying, measuring, recording, classifying); accounting takes over from there — summarising, analysing, interpreting, communicating.

questions.sourceRef: Book-keeping = primary stage; accounting = secondary stage beginning where book-keeping ends

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Subfields of accounting
questions.stem: The managers of Chennai Cotton Mills want cost and financial data reworked into whatever format helps next quarter's production decisions. The branch of accounting that serves this need is:

options.explanation: Financial accounting is largely historical and produces statements for OUTSIDE users in prescribed forms — not future-facing internal decision packs.
Correct. Management accounting reworks financial and cost data into whatever form managers need for planning and decisions — internal, future-facing, and bound by no prescribed format.
Cost accounting ascertains and controls the cost of products and activities — it supplies inputs, but the free-format decision reporting for managers is management accounting.
That branch reports the social costs and benefits of the business to society — nothing to do with internal production decisions.

questions.sourceRef: Management accounting: internal, future-facing, no prescribed format

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Book-keeping vs accounting
questions.stem: Which of the following tasks falls OUTSIDE the scope of book-keeping?

options.text: Recording credit sales in the sales book
options.explanation: Recording in books of original entry is core book-keeping.
Classifying entries in the ledger is still within book-keeping's routine scope.
Measuring in money terms is one of the four base activities book-keeping covers.

options.text: Interpreting what the profit-to-sales relationship means for the firm
options.explanation: Correct. Interpretation needs judgement and skill — it belongs to accounting, which begins where book-keeping's routine work ends.

questions.sourceRef: Book-keeping scope: identifying, measuring, recording, classifying only

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Users of financial statements
questions.stem: Which of the following is an INTERNAL user of Joshi Hardware's financial statements?

options.text: The bank that gave the firm a working-capital loan
options.explanation: Lenders are external users — they must rely on the published statements to judge whether interest and principal will arrive on time.

options.text: The management running the firm day to day
options.explanation: Correct. Internal users are the management (and owners running the business); everyone else reads the statements from outside.
Government and its agencies are external users — they use the statements for taxes, statistics and regulation.

options.text: A supplier who sells to the firm on two months' credit
options.explanation: Suppliers and trade creditors are external users, watching short-term paying capacity from outside.

questions.sourceRef: Internal users = management/owner-managers; all others external

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Users of financial statements
questions.stem: Agarwal Paper Mart supplies packaging to Deluxe Sweets on 60 days' credit. As a user of Deluxe Sweets' financial statements, Agarwal's PRIMARY interest is:

options.text: The long-term return Deluxe Sweets earns on its owner's capital
options.explanation: Return on capital is the investor's headline question — a trade creditor's money is locked in for weeks, not years.

options.text: The bonus and retirement benefits Deluxe Sweets can afford
options.explanation: That is the employees' and unions' angle on the statements, not a supplier's.

options.text: Whether Deluxe Sweets can clear its bills in the short run
options.explanation: Correct. Suppliers and trade creditors care first about short-term paying capacity — will the bill due in 60 days actually be paid?

options.text: The taxes Deluxe Sweets pays to the government
options.explanation: Tax collection is the government's interest as a user — irrelevant to whether a supplier's bill gets cleared.

questions.sourceRef: Suppliers/trade creditors: short-run liquidity focus

questions.stem: Meera pays her home's rent of ₹18,000 from the saree shop's cash box. In the shop's books this payment is recorded as:

options.explanation: Home rent is the owner's personal cost — charging it to the business mixes the owner with the entity and overstates business expenses.
Correct. Under the entity concept the business is separate from its owner; money the owner takes for personal use is drawings, never a business expense.
Nothing is owed to an outsider here — cash has already left for the owner's personal purpose.

options.text: Not recorded at all, since it is personal
options.explanation: Business cash DID go out, so the books must show it — as drawings reducing capital, not by ignoring the outflow.

questions.sourceRef: Entity concept: owner's personal use of business money = drawings

questions.stem: Kulkarni Foods buys a packing machine for ₹75,000 and, the same week, hires a brilliantly capable production manager. Only the machine enters the books. The concept at work is:

options.explanation: Correct. Accounting records only what money can measure — the machine has a price; the manager's skill has no reliable money value, so it stays out of the books.
The entity concept separates owner from business — nothing here involves the owner's personal dealings.
Prudence is about not anticipating profits and providing for probable losses — it does not decide WHAT is recordable.
Going concern assumes continuity of the business — it says nothing about whether an item is money-measurable.

questions.sourceRef: Money measurement: record only money-measurable items

questions.stem: Bansal Prints shows its printing machines at cost less depreciation, not at the price a scrap dealer would pay today. The assumption that justifies this is:

options.explanation: Prudence would, if anything, pull values DOWN toward caution — it is continuity, not caution, that keeps scrap values out of the picture.
Both cost and scrap value are money-measurable — that concept cannot choose between them.
Correct. Because the business is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future, assets are held for use — so they sit at cost less depreciation, and costs can be spread over future years at all.
Periodicity slices the business's life into years for reporting — it does not decide the valuation basis of machines.

questions.sourceRef: Going concern: assets at cost less depreciation, not liquidation value

questions.stem: Reddy Constructions bought land for ₹10,00,000 in 2020. The market value is now ₹45,00,000. Under the cost concept, the land appears in the books at:

options.explanation: Market appreciation is not recorded under the cost concept — writing the land up would also anticipate an unrealised gain.
Correct. An asset is recorded at its acquisition cost, and that cost remains the base for all later accounting — the market's opinion does not enter the books.
Averaging cost and market value is not an accounting treatment — the cost concept keeps the original figure, full stop.
The gain of ₹35,00,000 is the unrecorded appreciation, not a carrying value — and no part of it is recognised while the land is held.

questions.sourceRef: Cost concept: acquisition cost is the base; market rise ignored

questions.stem: The concept that gives every transaction two effects — and is therefore the seed of double-entry book-keeping and the equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital — is:

options.explanation: Matching pairs a period's revenues with the expenses incurred to earn them — a timing idea, not the two-effects idea.
Full disclosure is about revealing material information to users — nothing to do with the two-sided structure of entries.
Consistency asks for the same methods period after period — it does not explain why entries have two effects.
Correct. Every transaction has two sides — what comes in and where it came from — which keeps the accounting equation permanently in balance and underlies double entry.

questions.sourceRef: Dual aspect → Assets = Liabilities + Capital; basis of double entry

questions.stem: Salaries for March 2026 at Verghese Traders were paid only in April 2026. Under the accrual concept, the salaries belong to:

options.text: The year ending 31 March 2026, shown as outstanding salary
options.explanation: Correct. Accrual recognises an expense when it is INCURRED, not when cash moves — March's work was received in March, so the cost belongs to that year, with a liability for the unpaid amount.

options.text: The year 2026–27, because that is when cash was paid
options.explanation: That is cash-basis thinking — accrual deliberately ignores the payment date and follows the period in which the expense arose.

options.text: Whichever year the firm finds convenient
options.explanation: Expense timing is fixed by the accrual concept, not by convenience — otherwise profits could be steered at will.

options.text: Neither year — unpaid amounts are not recorded
options.explanation: Unpaid does not mean unrecorded — the whole point of accrual is that incurred-but-unpaid expenses enter the books as outstanding liabilities.

questions.sourceRef: Accrual: expense when incurred; outstanding salary example

questions.stem: Goods still unsold at year end are carried forward as closing stock instead of being charged to this year's Profit & Loss Account. The concept applied is:

options.explanation: Realisation stops revenue being recorded before sale — the closing-stock carry-forward is about the timing of the COST, which is matching's job.
Materiality separates significant items from trifles — it does not dictate carrying costs forward to meet future revenue.
Correct. Matching sets the period's revenues against the expenses incurred to earn THEM — the cost of unsold goods must wait to meet next year's sale, so it is carried forward as closing stock.
The entity concept separates owner from business — irrelevant to expense-revenue pairing.

questions.sourceRef: Matching: closing stock carried forward to meet next year's sale

questions.stem: In March 2026 Dhruv Electronics receives a confirmed order for 50 air-conditioners, to be delivered in May 2026. Recording this order as March revenue would violate:

options.explanation: Close cousin, wrong pick: accrual times expenses and incomes already earned or incurred. Here nothing is earned yet at all — the rule that blocks premature REVENUE is realisation.

Correct. Revenue is recorded only when realised — goods delivered and the legal right to receive established. A confirmed order with delivery still pending produces no revenue; profits are never anticipated.
Consistency is about using the same methods year after year — one premature sale entry is not a method-change issue.
Periodicity just slices life into years; it does not decide when a sale becomes a sale.

questions.sourceRef: Realisation: no revenue before delivery/legal right; advance order trap

questions.stem: Under the consistency concept, a firm may change an accounting method when:

options.text: Never — once chosen, a method is permanent
options.explanation: This overstates the rule. Consistency demands good reason and disclosure for a change, not a lifetime ban.

options.text: Whenever a different method would show a higher profit
options.explanation: Changing methods to dress up profit is exactly the abuse consistency exists to prevent.

options.text: Every year, to keep the accounts fresh
options.explanation: Routine annual switching would destroy comparability — the very quality consistency protects.

options.text: A statute or accounting standard requires it, or the new method presents the picture more appropriately — with disclosure
options.explanation: Correct. Consistency is not a freeze: change is allowed on those grounds, provided the change and its effect are disclosed so figures remain comparable.

questions.sourceRef: Consistency: change on statute/standard/more appropriate presentation, with disclosure

questions.stem: Which pair of practices are the two classic applications of the conservatism (prudence) convention?

options.text: Valuing inventory at lower of cost and net realisable value, and creating a provision for doubtful debts
options.explanation: Correct. Both anticipate no profit but provide for probable losses — the two textbook faces of prudence.

options.text: Recording assets at cost, and charging depreciation
options.explanation: Those flow from the cost concept and going concern/matching — routine allocation, not loss-anticipating caution.

options.text: Creating secret reserves, and deliberately understating profit
options.explanation: Deliberate understatement and secret reserves are ABUSES that distort the true and fair view — prudence never licenses them.

options.text: Recording anticipated profits, and ignoring possible losses
options.explanation: This is prudence stated exactly backwards on both halves.

questions.sourceRef: Prudence: LCNRV inventory + provision for doubtful debts; no secret reserves

questions.stem: A ₹450 stapler at Iyer Stores will serve for years, yet it is simply expensed in the year of purchase. The convention that permits this is:

options.explanation: Prudence is about probable losses and unanticipated profits — a ₹450 stapler is a question of significance, not caution.
Full disclosure asks that material information be revealed — this is the mirror-image case of an IMmaterial item.
Correct. Insignificant items do not deserve the ceremony of capitalisation and depreciation — materiality lets trifles be expensed, and significance is judged relative to the business.
Continuity of the business would, strictly, support spreading the cost — it is materiality that overrides the ceremony for tiny amounts.

questions.sourceRef: Materiality: trifles expensed; significance is relative

questions.stem: Chopping the indefinite life of a business into twelve-month slices so performance can be measured, compared and taxed on time follows the:

options.explanation: Going concern says the life IS indefinite; it is periodicity that then cuts that life into reporting slices. The two work together but answer different questions.
Correct. Periodicity divides the business's continuing life into equal accounting periods — normally a year — so results can be reported at regular intervals.
Matching works WITHIN a period, pairing its revenues and expenses — it presupposes the period that periodicity creates.
Dual aspect gives each transaction two effects — nothing to do with slicing time.

questions.sourceRef: Periodicity: equal accounting periods, normally one year

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · AS 1 fundamental assumptions
questions.stem: As per AS 1, the three fundamental accounting assumptions are:

options.explanation: Prudence is the classic smuggled-in wrong option — it belongs to AS 1's list of considerations for SELECTING accounting policies, not to the fundamental assumptions.
Matching and materiality never appear in the list of three — materiality is a policy-selection consideration and matching is a general concept.
Entity and money measurement are basic accounting concepts, but AS 1's fundamental assumptions are going concern, consistency and accrual.
Correct. AS 1 elevates exactly these three to fundamental accounting assumptions — nothing else makes the list.

questions.sourceRef: AS 1: fundamental assumptions = going concern, consistency, accrual

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · AS 1 fundamental assumptions
questions.stem: Patil Agencies follows all three fundamental accounting assumptions while preparing its statements. As per AS 1, regarding these assumptions the firm must:

options.text: Disclose specifically that each assumption has been followed
options.explanation: This reverses the rule — disclosure is demanded only on NON-observance; following the assumptions needs no announcement because readers assume them by default.
Correct. The rule is asymmetric: if the fundamental assumptions are followed, no specific disclosure is required; only a departure must be disclosed.

options.text: Obtain ICAI approval for following them
options.explanation: No approval mechanism exists — the assumptions are the default basis of preparation, not a permission.

options.text: Disclose them only if profits are affected
options.explanation: The disclosure test is observance versus non-observance, not the profit impact.

questions.sourceRef: AS 1: followed → no disclosure; not followed → disclose the fact

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · AS 1 fundamental assumptions
questions.stem: Fernandes Caterers keeps its books on a pure cash basis (recording incomes and expenses only when cash moves). As per AS 1, the firm:

options.text: Need not disclose anything, since cash basis is also an accepted method
options.explanation: Whatever its practical acceptance, cash basis departs from a FUNDAMENTAL assumption — and departures are exactly what AS 1 forces into the open.

options.text: Must disclose that going concern is not followed
options.explanation: Wrong assumption picked — cash-basis books abandon ACCRUAL; nothing here suggests the business will not continue.

options.text: Must disclose the fact, because the fundamental assumption of accrual is not being followed
options.explanation: Correct. Accrual is one of the three fundamental assumptions; when a fundamental assumption is not followed, that fact must be disclosed.
Consistency concerns using the same methods over time. A firm can be perfectly consistent about its cash basis — the assumption dropped is accrual.

questions.sourceRef: Cash basis = accrual not followed → disclosure required

questions.stem: The four PRINCIPAL qualitative characteristics that make financial statements useful are:

options.explanation: Correct. These four principal qualities together aim the statements at a true and fair view that users can actually use.
The first three are AS 1's fundamental ASSUMPTIONS (and prudence a policy-selection consideration) — assumptions about preparation, not qualities of the output.
Profitability, liquidity and solvency are things statements MEASURE about a business — not qualities of the information itself.
Prudence and materiality are ingredients (of reliability and relevance respectively), not two of the four principal characteristics.

questions.sourceRef: Four principal qualitative characteristics

questions.stem: Financial information that is free from material error and bias, faithfully represents what it claims to represent, and reports substance over legal form possesses the quality of:

options.explanation: Relevance is about whether the information helps users evaluate events or confirm earlier evaluations — usefulness of content, not trustworthiness of measurement.
Comparability is about usability against other years and other firms — it depends on consistency and disclosure, not on freedom from bias.
Understandability concerns presentation to a reasonably knowledgeable, diligent user — not the error-free, unbiased character of the numbers.
Correct. Freedom from material error and bias, faithful representation, substance over form, neutrality, prudence and completeness are the ingredients of reliability.

questions.sourceRef: Reliability: no material error/bias, faithful representation, substance over form

questions.stem: Within the qualitative characteristics framework, materiality operates as:

options.text: A fifth principal qualitative characteristic, equal in rank to the other four
options.explanation: The principal characteristics are four — understandability, relevance, reliability, comparability. Materiality serves INSIDE that framework as a threshold, not beside it.

options.text: The threshold of relevance — omitting or misstating an item matters when it could sway users' decisions
options.explanation: Correct. Materiality is not a free-standing principal quality here; it works as relevance's threshold, deciding which omissions or misstatements are big enough to matter.

options.text: A fundamental accounting assumption under AS 1
options.explanation: The AS 1 assumptions are going concern, consistency and accrual — materiality appears in AS 1 only among the policy-SELECTION considerations.
The measurement bases are historical cost, current cost, realisable value and present value — materiality is about significance, not valuation.

questions.sourceRef: Materiality = threshold of relevance

questions.stem: Kavya starts Lotus Boutique with cash ₹5,00,000. She then (i) buys shelving for ₹1,20,000 cash, (ii) buys fabric on credit from Ganga Textiles for ₹2,00,000, and (iii) sells fabric costing ₹60,000 for ₹85,000 cash. Total assets of the business after these transactions are:

options.explanation: This keeps stock at the full ₹2,00,000 — the goods costing ₹60,000 that were sold must come OUT of stock (their value now sits in the cash received).
This is the CAPITAL balance (5,00,000 + profit 25,000), not total assets — the creditor-financed assets are missing from the count.
This records the sale at cost (₹60,000 into cash instead of ₹85,000) — the ₹25,000 profit earned on the sale is part of the business's assets too.

questions.sourceRef: Assets = Liabilities + Capital; equation built transaction by transaction

questions.stem: On 31 March 2026 Rohan's business shows: machinery ₹3,20,000; stock ₹1,50,000; debtors ₹90,000; cash ₹40,000; creditors ₹1,10,000; bank loan ₹80,000. Rohan's capital is:

options.explanation: This is TOTAL ASSETS — the outsiders' claims (creditors and bank loan) must be deducted before what belongs to the owner is left.
This deducts only the creditors and forgets the bank loan of ₹80,000 — a loan is just as much an outside liability as a trade creditor.
This ADDS the liabilities to assets instead of subtracting them — the equation is Capital = Assets MINUS Liabilities.

questions.sourceRef: Capital = Assets − Liabilities

questions.stem: Sanjana's closing capital on 31 March 2026 is ₹3,80,000 and her opening capital was ₹3,00,000. During the year she withdrew ₹45,000 for personal use and introduced fresh capital of ₹50,000. Her profit for the year is:

options.explanation: This forgets to deduct the fresh capital of ₹50,000 — money the owner put IN is not profit the business earned, so it must be stripped out of the capital increase.
This SUBTRACTS the drawings instead of adding them back (3,80,000 − 3,00,000 − 50,000 − 45,000). Drawings already reduced closing capital, so they are added back to find the profit actually earned.
This is just the raw rise in capital (3,80,000 − 3,00,000) — it ignores both the drawings taken out and the fresh capital put in.
Correct. Profit = Closing capital − Opening capital − Fresh capital + Drawings = 3,80,000 − 3,00,000 − 50,000 + 45,000 = ₹75,000.

questions.sourceRef: Profit = closing capital − opening capital − additional capital + drawings

questions.stem: Farhan's opening capital was ₹2,60,000. During the year he earned a profit of ₹96,000 and introduced fresh capital of ₹40,000. His closing capital on 31 March 2026 is ₹3,44,000. His drawings for the year were:

options.explanation: This ignores the fresh capital of ₹40,000 (2,60,000 + 96,000 − 3,44,000) — the owner's new contribution raised capital too, so more must have been withdrawn to land at ₹3,44,000.
Correct. Drawings = Opening capital + Fresh capital + Profit − Closing capital = 2,60,000 + 40,000 + 96,000 − 3,44,000 = ₹52,000.
This adds the fresh capital to the CLOSING side instead of the opening side ((3,44,000 + 40,000) − (2,60,000 + 96,000)) — a direction slip on where the contribution belongs.
This SUBTRACTS the profit instead of adding it (2,60,000 + 40,000 − 96,000 gives 2,04,000; 3,44,000 − 2,04,000 = 1,40,000) — profit increases capital, it never reduces it.

questions.sourceRef: Closing capital = Opening + Additional + Profit − Drawings, rearranged for drawings

questions.stem: Thomas Traders buys goods worth ₹1,20,000 on credit from Malabar Wholesale. The effect on the accounting equation is:

options.text: One asset increases and another decreases — totals unchanged
options.explanation: That is the CASH purchase pattern (stock up, cash down). Nothing was paid here — a liability was created instead.
Capital moves only for the owner's contributions, incomes, expenses and drawings — buying on credit involves an outsider's claim, not the owner's.

options.text: Assets increase ₹1,20,000 and liabilities increase ₹1,20,000 — totals grow on both sides
options.explanation: Correct. Stock (an asset) rises and a creditor (a liability) arises for the same amount — the equation grows equally on both sides and stays balanced.
No expense has occurred — goods worth the full amount came in, so it is an ASSET that rises against the new liability, and capital is untouched.

questions.sourceRef: Credit purchase: assets ↑ and liabilities ↑ equally

questions.stem: Before a payment, Qureshi Traders shows total assets ₹5,00,000, liabilities ₹1,80,000 and capital ₹3,20,000. The firm then pays a creditor ₹30,000 by cheque. After the payment, total assets and total liabilities respectively are:

options.explanation: Correct. Bank (asset) falls by 30,000 and the creditor (liability) falls by 30,000 — both sides shrink equally and capital stays at ₹3,20,000: 4,70,000 = 1,50,000 + 3,20,000.
This cancels the liability without paying anything out — but the cheque means bank balance (an asset) fell by the same ₹30,000.
This records the cash outflow but leaves the creditor standing — the payment extinguishes the liability; otherwise the equation would break by ₹30,000.
This treats the payment as an EXPENSE hitting capital — paying a creditor settles an existing claim; nothing is consumed, so capital is untouched.

questions.sourceRef: Paying a creditor: assets ↓ and liabilities ↓ equally; capital unchanged

questions.stem: Meera pays the shop's electricity bill of ₹8,000 in cash. In equation terms, the second effect (besides cash falling) is:

options.explanation: No liability existed for this bill in the books — an expense paid in cash reduces CAPITAL, not liabilities. (Liabilities fall only when a recorded creditor is settled.)
Electricity is consumed, not acquired — nothing of lasting value comes in to stand as an asset.
Paying cash creates no new obligation — a liability would arise only if the bill were left UNPAID.
Correct. Expenses and losses pull capital down — the owner's stake absorbs every cost of running the business. Assets ↓ 8,000 · Capital ↓ 8,000.

questions.sourceRef: Expenses reduce capital, not liabilities

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Capital vs revenue expenditure
questions.stem: Arjun Textiles spends during the year: new power loom ₹4,00,000; carriage on the loom ₹18,000; installation charges ₹22,000; annual maintenance contract ₹15,000; repainting the factory gate ₹6,000; adding a new room to the workshop ₹1,50,000. Total CAPITAL expenditure is:

options.explanation: This capitalises the loom, carriage and installation but leaves out the workshop extension of ₹1,50,000 — adding a room extends capacity, a classic capital item.
This capitalises EVERYTHING, including the maintenance contract and gate repainting — routine upkeep whose benefit ends within the year is revenue expenditure.
Correct. Loom 4,00,000 + carriage 18,000 + installation 22,000 (costs of bringing it to working condition) + new room 1,50,000 (extends capacity) = ₹5,90,000. Maintenance and repainting are revenue.
This takes only the loom and the extension, expensing carriage and installation — but costs of bringing an asset to working condition form part of its capital cost.

questions.sourceRef: Capital expenditure: acquire + bring to working condition + extend capacity

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Capital vs revenue expenditure
questions.stem: Menon Motors spends during the year: engine overhaul of an in-use delivery van, restoring its normal working, ₹48,000; annual insurance ₹12,000; wages for the year ₹1,20,000; a new hydraulic lift ₹2,20,000; whitewashing the workshop ₹8,000. Total REVENUE expenditure is:

options.explanation: This capitalises the ₹48,000 overhaul because it looks heavy — but repairs to an asset already in use that merely RESTORE normal working are revenue regardless of the bill's size.
Correct. Overhaul of an in-use van 48,000 (restores existing capacity — size does not matter) + insurance 12,000 + wages 1,20,000 + whitewashing 8,000 = ₹1,88,000. Only the new lift is capital.
This includes the hydraulic lift — acquiring a new fixed asset is capital expenditure, never part of the year's revenue charge.
This drops the wages of ₹1,20,000 — wages and salaries for the year are the running cost of the period, squarely revenue expenditure.

questions.sourceRef: Revenue expenditure: run, maintain, restore; in-use repairs revenue regardless of size

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Capital vs revenue expenditure
questions.stem: Bafna Mills spends ₹5,00,000 on repairs that only restore an old machine's normal working, and ₹30,000 on an attachment that permanently raises the machine's output. The correct classification is:

options.explanation: This classifies by amount — the big bill capitalised, the small one expensed. Size is not a classification test; the benefit's nature is.

options.text: Both capital, since both relate to a fixed asset
options.explanation: Touching a fixed asset does not make spending capital — running and maintaining an existing asset is revenue expenditure.

options.text: Both revenue, since both were paid this year
options.explanation: When payment happens is irrelevant — the attachment's benefit (higher capacity) lasts beyond the period, making it capital.
Correct. Judge the NATURE of the benefit, never the size of the bill: restoring existing capacity is revenue even at ₹5,00,000; permanently raising earning capacity is capital even at ₹30,000.

questions.sourceRef: Nature of benefit, not size of bill, decides capital vs revenue

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Capital vs revenue receipts
questions.stem: Prakash Traders receives during the year: sale of goods ₹8,20,000; sale of an old delivery van ₹65,000; bank loan ₹3,00,000; insurance claim for machinery destroyed in a fire ₹90,000; commission earned ₹25,000; fresh capital from the owner ₹1,50,000. Total CAPITAL receipts are:

options.explanation: Correct. Van sale 65,000 (fixed asset) + bank loan 3,00,000 (liability created) + machinery insurance claim 90,000 (replaces a fixed asset) + fresh capital 1,50,000 = ₹6,05,000. None of this is income.
This treats the machinery insurance claim as a revenue receipt — but a claim for a destroyed FIXED ASSET is capital; only a claim for destroyed STOCK is revenue.
This adds the commission of ₹25,000 — commission earned is income of the period, a revenue receipt belonging to the P&L.
This leaves out the owner's fresh capital of ₹1,50,000 — capital brought in is the textbook capital receipt; it goes to the balance sheet, never the P&L.

questions.sourceRef: Capital receipts: owner's capital, loans, fixed-asset sale proceeds, fixed-asset insurance claims

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Capital vs revenue receipts
questions.stem: A fire at Goyal Traders destroys both a machine and a godown full of stock. The insurer pays two claims — one for the machine, one for the stock. The correct classification of the two receipts is:

options.text: Both capital receipts, since both came from the insurer
options.explanation: The payer's identity is irrelevant — classification follows WHAT the receipt replaces: a fixed asset versus trading stock.

options.text: Both revenue receipts, since both arose this year
options.explanation: Timing does not decide the split — the machine claim stands in the shoes of a fixed asset and is therefore capital.

options.text: Machine claim — capital receipt; stock claim — revenue receipt
options.explanation: Correct. The machine claim replaces a fixed asset, so it is capital; the stock claim replaces trading goods and is set against the trading loss, so it is revenue.

options.text: Machine claim — revenue; stock claim — capital
options.explanation: Exactly reversed — fixed asset → capital, stock → revenue. Swapping them misstates both the P&L and the balance sheet.

questions.sourceRef: Insurance claims: machine → capital receipt; stock → revenue receipt

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Capital vs revenue expenditure
questions.stem: Bhavna Engineering buys a second-hand lathe for ₹1,80,000, pays freight of ₹12,000 to bring it to the factory, spends ₹35,000 overhauling it BEFORE first use, and pays ₹60,000 as operating labour for the first year of running it. The amount capitalised as the cost of the lathe is:

options.explanation: This expenses the ₹35,000 overhaul as if it were ordinary repairs — but an overhaul BEFORE first use is what makes the second-hand asset usable at all, so it is capitalised.
This capitalises the first year's operating labour too — running costs after the asset is in use are revenue expenditure, however close they sit to the purchase.
This takes the bare price only — freight and the pre-use overhaul are both costs of bringing the asset to working condition and belong in its capital cost.

Correct. Price 1,80,000 + freight 12,000 + pre-use overhaul 35,000 = ₹2,27,000 — everything needed to bring the lathe to working condition is capital. The operating labour is a running cost of the period.

questions.sourceRef: Pre-use overhaul of second-hand asset capitalised; running costs revenue

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Deferred revenue expenditure
questions.stem: Havelis Foods spends a massive one-time amount on a nationwide launch campaign whose benefit will run for several years. Under the SM's classic treatment, the unwritten-off balance of this deferred revenue expenditure appears in the balance sheet as:

options.explanation: Prepaid rent buys a definite, enforceable future service; DRE carries no such claim — the campaign money is spent with only an EXPECTED future benefit. The two are different items.

options.text: A fictitious asset on the asset side
options.explanation: Correct. DRE is revenue in nature but spread over its benefit years; the balance not yet written off sits on the asset side as a fictitious asset — no real value stands behind it.

options.text: A fixed asset, depreciated over its life
options.explanation: Nothing tangible or legally protected was acquired — the spending is revenue in NATURE; only its charging is postponed.
The money has been PAID, not owed — there is no obligation to show; the leftover balance is an asset-side (fictitious) item.

questions.sourceRef: DRE: written off over benefit years; balance = fictitious asset (SM classic treatment)

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Provisions vs contingent liabilities
questions.stem: Wadhwa Appliances (i) expects warranty claims on this year's sales — outflow probable and reliably estimable — and (ii) is defending a court case it may possibly lose. The correct treatment is:

options.text: (i) recognise a provision in the accounts; (ii) disclose a contingent liability in the notes
options.explanation: Correct. Probable + reliably estimable = provision, recognised in the accounts. Merely possible, hinging on an uncertain future event = contingent liability, disclosed in the notes only.

options.text: (i) disclose in notes; (ii) recognise a provision
options.explanation: Swapped — the warranty obligation already exists and is estimable (provision); the court case is only a POSSIBLE obligation (contingent, notes only).

options.text: Recognise both as liabilities in the accounts
options.explanation: Recording the merely-possible court loss overstates liabilities — a contingent liability is never recorded, only disclosed.

options.text: Ignore both until cash actually flows out
options.explanation: That is cash-basis thinking — the probable, estimable warranty outflow must be provided for now (prudence and accrual both demand it).

questions.sourceRef: Provision = probable + estimable, recognised; contingent liability = possible, disclosed only

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Provisions vs contingent liabilities
questions.stem: Lakhani Traders has discounted bills receivable with its bank that have not yet matured and may possibly be dishonoured. In the financial statements these bills are:

options.text: Recorded as a liability in the balance sheet
options.explanation: Recording assumes the outflow is probable — a discounted bill creates only a POSSIBLE obligation, which is disclosed, never recorded.
A provision needs a present obligation with a probable, estimable outflow — mere possibility of dishonour does not meet that bar.

options.text: Disclosed in the notes as a contingent liability
options.explanation: Correct. Bills discounted that may bounce are the exam's staple contingent liability — the obligation hangs on an uncertain future event (dishonour), so they live in the notes, not the accounts.

options.text: Omitted entirely, since the bank now holds the bills
options.explanation: Handing the bills over does not end the firm's exposure — if the acceptor dishonours, the bank recovers from the firm; users must be told of that possibility.

questions.sourceRef: Bills discounted = contingent liability in notes

questions.stem: Rathi Mills decides to (i) depreciate machinery by the Written Down Value method, and (ii) treat the machinery's useful life as eight years. In AS 1 terms, these two decisions are respectively:

options.text: (i) an accounting estimate; (ii) an accounting policy
options.explanation: Swapped — this word-swap is the whole trick in the question. The method is the policy; the numeric life is the estimate.

options.text: (i) an accounting policy; (ii) an accounting estimate
options.explanation: Correct. Choosing the WDV METHOD is a policy (a principle plus its method of application); judging the life at EIGHT YEARS is an estimate — an approximation revised prospectively when facts change.
The eight-year life is not a chosen principle but an approximation of the unknowable — revising it is not a policy change and needs no policy-change justification.
The depreciation method is a deliberate choice among accepted alternatives — that is a policy, disclosed with the firm's other policies.

questions.sourceRef: Method = policy; useful life = estimate (revised prospectively)

questions.stem: As per AS 1, the three considerations that govern the SELECTION of accounting policies are:

options.explanation: Those are AS 1's fundamental ASSUMPTIONS — the other famous list of three. Swapping the two lists is the classic exam trap.
Those are qualitative characteristics of the finished statements, not AS 1's stated considerations for choosing policies.
Those are basic accounting concepts from the general framework — AS 1's policy-selection trio is prudence, substance over form and materiality.
Correct. These three guide policy selection, all in service of a true and fair view — e.g. substance over form puts a hire-purchase asset in the buyer's books before legal title passes.

questions.sourceRef: AS 1 policy-selection considerations: prudence, substance over form, materiality

questions.stem: Carrying an asset at today's discounted value of the future net cash inflows it is expected to generate means measuring it at:

options.explanation: Historical cost is what was PAID when the asset was acquired — the everyday base, looking backward, with no discounting involved.
Current cost asks what acquiring the same asset TODAY would cost — a replacement question, not a discounted-cash-flow question.
Correct. Present value discounts the asset's expected future net cash inflows back to today — one of the four measurement bases.
Realisable (settlement) value is what an orderly sale would fetch today — an exit price, not a discounted stream of future inflows.

questions.sourceRef: Measurement bases: historical cost, current cost, realisable value, present value

questions.stem: Define accounting and state the steps of the accounting process in order, indicating where recording, classifying and summarising respectively take place. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Definition: process of identifying money-measurable transactions/events, recording, classifying and summarising them, and analysing, interpreting and communicating the results to users (classic AICPA-style definition)
Steps in order: identifying → measuring → recording → classifying → summarising → analysing → interpreting → communicating
Recording happens in the journal and subsidiary books (books of original entry)
Classifying happens in the ledger (like entries grouped in one account)
Summarising produces the trial balance and then the P&L Account and Balance Sheet

questions.sourceRef: Accounting definition + eight steps + stage locations

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Book-keeping vs accounting
questions.stem: Distinguish between book-keeping and accounting on any four points, and name the branch of accounting that serves internal management decisions. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Scope: book-keeping — identifying, measuring, recording, classifying; accounting — also summarising, analysing, interpreting, communicating
Stage: book-keeping is the primary (base) stage; accounting is secondary — it begins where book-keeping ends

Objective: book-keeping maintains systematic records; accounting shows results and financial position to users. Nature: book-keeping routine/clerical; accounting analytical, needing judgement and skill
Branch serving internal management decisions: management accounting — internal, future-facing, bound by no prescribed format

questions.sourceRef: Book-keeping vs accounting distinctions; management accounting

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · AS 1 fundamental assumptions
questions.stem: Name the three fundamental accounting assumptions per AS 1 and explain the disclosure requirement attached to them. A firm maintains its accounts on cash basis — what must it do, and why? (5 marks)

skeleton.point: The three fundamental accounting assumptions: going concern, consistency, accrual
Disclosure rule (asymmetric): if the assumptions are followed, no specific disclosure is required — readers assume them by default
If any fundamental assumption is NOT followed, that fact must be disclosed
Cash-basis firm: must disclose the fact, because accrual — a fundamental assumption — is not being followed; brief reason (incomes/expenses recognised on receipt/payment, not when earned/incurred)

questions.sourceRef: AS 1: three assumptions + disclosure-on-departure

questions.stem: Explain any five of the following concepts with one example each: entity, going concern, accrual, matching, realisation, prudence. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Entity: business separate from owner; capital is a liability of the business toward the owner; owner's personal payments from business cash = drawings (e.g. home rent from the shop's cash box)
Going concern: continuity assumed for the foreseeable future; assets at cost less depreciation rather than scrap value; costs can be spread over future years
Accrual: revenue when earned, expense when incurred, not when cash moves (e.g. March salaries paid in April → outstanding salary of March's year)

Matching: period's revenues set against expenses incurred to earn them (e.g. unsold goods carried forward as closing stock to meet next year's sale). Realisation (alternative): revenue only when realised — confirmed advance order produces no revenue; profits never anticipated
Prudence: anticipate no profit, provide for all probable losses (e.g. inventory at lower of cost and NRV; provision for doubtful debts); does not permit secret reserves

questions.sourceRef: Core concepts with micro-examples

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Capital vs revenue
questions.stem: State the tests that distinguish capital expenditure from revenue expenditure, and classify with one-line reasons: (i) overhaul of a second-hand machine before first use; (ii) heavy repairs to an in-use machine restoring normal working; (iii) legal fees to purchase land; (iv) annual whitewashing. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Tests: (1) does the benefit last beyond the current accounting period? (2) does it acquire a fixed asset / bring it to working condition / increase earning capacity — or merely run/maintain/restore what exists? Acquire, install, extend, improve → capital; run, maintain, restore → revenue
(i) Overhaul before first use — capital: needed to make the asset usable at all, part of bringing it to working condition
(ii) Heavy in-use repairs restoring normal working — revenue: maintains existing capacity; size of the bill is never the test
(iii) Legal fees to purchase land — capital: part of the acquisition cost of the asset
(iv) Annual whitewashing — revenue: routine upkeep, benefit exhausted within the year

questions.sourceRef: Capital vs revenue expenditure tests + classification battery

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Theoretical Framework · Provisions, contingents & DRE
questions.stem: Distinguish between a provision and a contingent liability, giving one example of each. Also state the meaning and treatment of deferred revenue expenditure per the SM. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Provision: present liability whose amount must be estimated — outflow probable and reliably estimable — RECOGNISED in the accounts (e.g. provision for doubtful debts, warranty claims)

Contingent liability: only a possible obligation hinging on an uncertain future event, or outflow not probable/not reliably measurable — NOT recorded, only DISCLOSED in the notes (e.g. bills discounted that may bounce; pending court case)
DRE meaning: expenditure revenue in nature but so large and forward-reaching that one year's charge would distort results (e.g. massive one-time launch campaign)
DRE treatment: write off over the years of expected benefit; unwritten-off balance shown on the asset side as a fictitious asset

questions.sourceRef: Provision vs contingent liability; DRE meaning and treatment
